newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia will allow 400,000 T 1997 wheat imports.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia will allow 400,000 T 1997 wheat imports.

text.p: The Yugoslav government will allow up to 400,000 tonnes of imported wheat to enter the country in 1997, but actual wheat imports are seen below the set quota, a senior government official said on Wednesday.
"Based on Yugoslavia's commodity inventories, the government has set a 1997 import quota at 400,000 tonnes of wheat," Yugoslav trade minister Djordje Siradovic told Reuters.
"But we expect better crop this year and hope not to import as much wheat. We just need to overbridge a few months gap till this year's harvest," Siradovic said.
Yugoslavia, facing an acute grain shortage after its worst harvest in 25 years, increased its wheat area to about 850,000 hectares in 1996 from 583,000 hectares in 1995.
Last year, the country produced only 1.5 million tonnes of wheat, after 2.97 million tonnes in 1995.
The government said it would not act as an importer as its stocks were sufficient, but it would approve any commercial deals.
"Importing wheat is very profitable now. The local price of wheat is very high due to the present shortage," the head of the Yugoslav grains fund, Vukosav Sakovic, said.
The fund estimates that some 70,000 tonnes of imported wheat have already entered the country.
"This is far less than we'd expected, but bad weather and ice on the Danube during Christmas and New Year holidays delayed those shipments," Sakovic said.
Another 200,000-300,000 tonnes were seen reaching the country within the next three months.
"The government would like to end the whole business by early May. But it is highly unlikely that the importers would agree to give up such a lucrative investment," Sakovic said.
Commodity specialists said the market surplus of domestic wheat was negligible. "It appears very seldom on the market," said an expert who asked not to be named.
"But right now, there is more wheat supply than 10-15 days ago. It came from Argentina and sells between 1.6 and 1.5 dinars per kg," the source said.

Yugoslavia needs around 500,000 tonnes of wheat to secure an estimated 2.5 million tonnes to feed its 10.5 million people and some 500,000 refugees, analysts said. --Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
